name: Adam Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Adam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential and your name won't be attached to it, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself and how you came to line work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, and I'm a second-year apprentice, which still sounds funny to say out loud at my age. I drove a forklift at a supermarket distribution centre for sixteen years and I was the union steward there for the last eight. When the city electricity company opened an adult entry scheme three years ago, the union pushed it hard, and I thought, this is a trade, this is a pension, this is something they can't ship overseas. Lena, my partner, is a ward nurse, and we've got Milo, who's twelve, and Ivy, who's nine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We're in the yard by half six, safety talk with Darek, our foreman, then out in the bucket truck to whatever's on the sheet: a rotten pole on Station Road, a transformer swap, a new service drop to somebody's extension. I'm the one handing up tools, rigging the ropes, digging, and slowly being let up the pole for the simpler jobs. I love the end of a job when the lights come back on and some old lady waves from her window. What wears me out is being the slowest one on the crew at 43, with lads of 25 telling me my knot's wrong, and they're usually right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Here's the card: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, which is that I told you so. Every few years somebody on the telly says the robots are coming, and the poles on Station Road are still wood and still rotting. At the union meeting I'd probably make a joke about it and move on to the overtime rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I get to finish what I started. I didn't retrain at 40 to get pushed out at 45, so a quiet, boring future suits me fine. I'd get my ticket, do my twenty years and hand the truck keys to somebody younger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and over the next year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep at my apprenticeship modules, pass the climbing assessment in the spring, and keep putting a bit aside every month like we already do. Maybe I'd finally stop reading those articles Lena sends me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AI Plateau?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. It's like a storm warning that turns out to be drizzle. You've already tied everything down, and then you just get on with your day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop reading the articles Lena sends. What are they usually about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh, all sorts, robots in hospitals, AI writing nurses' notes, that kind of thing. She's more worried for her job than I am for mine, which is backwards if you ask me, because nobody's replacing a nurse who holds your hand at three in the morning. I don't open the links half the time, I just say 'mm' and put the kettle on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing much changes, is there anything you'd miss about all the talk of change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Miss it? No. Well, maybe one thing. The young lads on the crew talk about drones doing the line patrols, and part of me would have liked to see the company spend money on the network instead of on consultants. If AI is just hype, the money goes back into the same old pockets and the poles still rot.

S0.say: He'd say he always knew the robot talk was overblown and that the poles on Station Road are still wood. At the union meeting it would be a joke and then back to the overtime rota.
S0.think: He thinks a quiet future lets him finish the trade he started at 40 and do his twenty years. He didn't retrain to be pushed out again, so boring suits him.
S0.do: Keeps working through his apprenticeship modules and aims to pass the climbing assessment in the spring. Keeps saving the same monthly amount and changes nothing else.
S0.feel: Relieved, like a storm warning that turns into drizzle.
S0.quote: It's like a storm warning that turns out to be drizzle. You've already tied everything down, and then you just get on with your day.
S0.fieldNote: Adam's whole bet was that line work is safe from change, so this picture simply confirms it. He brushes off Lena's worry about her own job a little too quickly. The one note of regret is political: he'd like money to go into the network rather than consultants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, right, then this is what the union is for. If tasks are changing, we sit down with management and we write it into the agreement: who gets trained, who gets moved, nobody gets binned. Online I don't post much, but I'd share the union's statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not that worried about the climbing side, because a pole in somebody's back garden is a mess no machine likes. What worries me is the office side, the job sheets and the planning, because once a computer plans the day, it also decides how many of us are needed on the truck. I'm the junior, so I'm the one that sentence is about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stand for the health and safety committee next year, because that's where these decisions really get made. I'd keep my head down and pass every module first time, so nobody has an excuse. And I'd tell Lena we keep the savings where they are, we don't touch them for a new car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing Steady Disruption?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I know. I've been through change at the warehouse when they brought in the scanners and the voice picking. You feel it in your stomach, then you get organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the warehouse. What happened when the scanners came in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They told us it would make our lives easier, and it did, for about a month. Then the targets went up, and the scanner was timing your toilet breaks. We fought it as a branch and got the targets eased, but two older blokes left within the year, and one of them, Frank, never worked again. That's what I think of when somebody says 'tasks change'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use any of the new tools yourself, if they came to your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company hands me a tablet and says this is how you log a job now, I'll use it, I'm not daft. But I won't go playing with chatbots at home to get ahead, no. I'd rather Darek show me how to splice a cable properly than have a phone tell me.

S1.say: He'd say this is exactly what the union is for and that changes should be written into the agreement so nobody gets binned. Online he'd only share the union's statement.
S1.think: He believes climbing work in back gardens is hard for machines, but he worries that computer-planned job sheets will cut crew sizes. As the junior, he expects to be the first one cut.
S1.do: Stands for the health and safety committee next year and makes sure he passes every module first time. Keeps the family savings untouched instead of buying a new car.
S1.feel: Uneasy, in a familiar way from the warehouse days, a knot in the stomach that turns into getting organised.
S1.quote: They told us it would make our lives easier, and it did, for about a month. Then the targets went up, and the scanner was timing your toilet breaks.
S1.fieldNote: His fear isn't the robot on the pole but the planning software that decides crew size. The warehouse story about Frank is the emotional core of how he reads change. He'll use tools only when told to, never on his own time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd be loud about it. I'd say this is the biggest grab in history, a few companies owning the robots and everybody else told to be grateful. I'd be at every union meeting and I'd be writing to our councillor, because the electricity company is owned by the city and the city answers to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm scared. I'm 43, I'm the least experienced man on the crew, and I'd be retraining for the second time in five years into, what, exactly? We've got the money to last a while, but money in the bank isn't a reason to get up in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with Lena and work out exactly how long we last on her wage plus the rent from Dad's flat, without my pay. I'd stop the extra overpayments on the mortgage and keep the cash where we can reach it. And I'd push the union to demand that the city keeps human crews on the network for safety, at least for live work, while we fight for some kind of share of what the machines earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like being on the pole when the wind picks up and you can't get down quick. You hold on, you keep your breathing slow, but your hands are shaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said two years. What does having only two years do to you, compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. It's not even my apprenticeship. I wouldn't have time to finish the thing I started, let alone learn the next thing, so it'd be all fight and no plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Milo and Ivy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth in small bits. Milo would ask if I'm losing my job, because he hears everything, and I'd say maybe, but Mum and I have saved for exactly this, and nobody's losing the house. Ivy would just want to know if we can still go camping in the summer, and I'd say yes, because camping is cheap.

S2.say: He'd call it the biggest grab in history and push hard through the union and the city council, since the electricity company is publicly owned. He'd be loud and public about it.
S2.think: He's scared: he's the least experienced on the crew and would face a second retraining in five years with no clear target. Savings buy time but not a reason to get up in the morning.
S2.do: Works out with Lena how long they can last on her wage and the flat's rent. Stops extra mortgage payments to keep cash at hand, and pushes the union and council to keep human crews on live work and win a share of machine earnings.
S2.feel: Scared and shaky but holding on, like being on a pole when the wind picks up.
S2.quote: Money in the bank isn't a reason to get up in the morning.
S2.fieldNote: His strong savings blunt the money fear but not the fear of being useless at 43. He reaches immediately for collective and political tools, which is where he feels competent. The two-year timeline hits him hard because it's shorter than his own apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's not waste them shouting. Use them to get proper rules in place before it lands: notice periods, retraining paid by the companies, and the city keeping a public stake in whatever robots work our network. I'd say that at the union and I'd say it to anyone at the school gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd probably get my full ticket and a couple of years as a qualified lineman. That's something. But it also means I'd be 48 when it hits, and I'm not going to be the bloke learning computers at 48, I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship, no question, and I'd put whatever overtime I get straight into savings. I'd get more involved in the union nationally, not just our branch, because a branch can't win this alone. And Lena and I would sort out Dad's flat properly, maybe do it up, so the rent covers more of the mortgage if my wage goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to do with my hands. Five years gives me a job list, and I'm better with a job list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't be learning computers at 48. Is that a choice or a worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both, if I'm honest. I watched Frank try to do an online course after the warehouse, and he'd ring me to ask where the 'any key' was. I don't want to be Frank, but I'm closer to Frank than to those lads on my crew who talk to their phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you could only win one thing through the union in those five years, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That nobody with ten or more years left gets thrown out without being paid while they retrain. Not a handout, a wage, because we built the network the robots will be working on. If I got that, I'd sleep.

S3.say: He'd say five years should be used to get rules in place, not wasted shouting: notice periods, company-paid retraining and a public stake in the robots that work the network.
S3.think: He thinks five years lets him qualify and work a couple of years as a lineman, but he doubts he'd learn something new at 48. He knows his own limits with technology.
S3.do: Finishes the apprenticeship and puts all overtime into savings. Gets involved in the union at national level and does up his late father's flat so the rent covers more of the mortgage.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadier, because five years gives him a job list.
S3.quote: I don't want to be Frank, but I'm closer to Frank than to those lads on my crew who talk to their phones.
S3.fieldNote: Adam is honest about his own resistance to learning new technology and names it without shame. The extra time turns panic into a to-do list, mostly collective. His one demand, paid retraining, is framed as earned, not charity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and if we waste it, that's on the government and the companies, not on workers. I'd want the union to have a proper plan by year two, not year nine. I'd probably even say it on the local radio if they asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I'd have done most of a career in this trade, and I'd be 53. That's still young enough that I'd need something. But there's part of me that thinks ten years is far enough away that it might not happen at all, and I'd catch myself waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, I'd do the job, and I'd keep saving. Around year five I'd look at whether the union can get older lineworkers into the jobs that'll still need a person, like safety sign-off or training the young ones. I'd want Milo to think hard about a trade versus university, because I genuinely don't know which is safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. It's a long way off, and I'm good at putting things in a box until they're closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd catch yourself waiting. What would make you stop waiting and act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing one on our network. Not on the telly, on our network. The day Darek tells me a robot did a pole change on Station Road, I'll stop waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this picture where you come out better off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if the unions win and the gains get shared. If the robots do the dangerous stuff and the rest of us work fewer hours on the same pay, I'd take that. I just don't trust anyone who owns the robots to offer it without a fight.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is a gift and wasting it would be on the government and companies. He wants the union to have a plan by year two and would say so on local radio.
S4.think: He sees ten years as most of a career in the trade but knows he'd still need something at 53. Part of him suspects it might not happen at all, and he'd catch himself waiting.
S4.do: Qualifies, works and keeps saving, then around year five pushes the union to steer older lineworkers into safety and training roles. Talks with Milo about trade versus university.
S4.feel: Uneasy rather than scared, because he can box it up until it's closer.
S4.quote: The day Darek tells me a robot did a pole change on Station Road, I'll stop waiting.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Adam drifts towards waiting, which he admits openly. The trigger he names is concrete and local, not news. He can picture a good outcome, but only one won through a fight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't enough to finish anything, and I'd be the junior bloke with no trade and no plan. What would help is the union and the city deciding up front that nobody on the network gets dumped without a paid wage while they retrain, and maybe somebody sitting with me in person, not on a website, to work out what I'm actually good for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Lena, and you should have. Everyone says nurses are safe, but if the hospital goes, it's both of us at once, and then the savings are all we've got. I think about that more than about my own job, if I'm honest.

headlineQuote: I didn't retrain at 40 to get pushed out at 45, so a quiet, boring future suits me fine.
portrait: Adam Novak is a 43-year-old second-year apprentice lineworker on a city-owned electricity company crew, after sixteen years driving a forklift and serving as a union steward. He chose the trade because it felt safe from change, and he has solid savings plus rent from his late father's flat. He reads every scenario through the warehouse, where new scanners raised targets and pushed older colleagues out. He stays calm in the plateau, turns to the union in steady change, and becomes alarmed by fast AGI because he'd be the junior man with no time to finish his trade. Given more warning, he makes lists and fights for paid retraining, but admits he won't learn computers late and might simply wait.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years is shorter than his apprenticeship and he'd be the junior lineworker with no trade and no plan.
whatWouldHelp: A guarantee from the union and the city that no one on the network is dropped without a paid wage while they retrain, and in-person help working out what he's good for.
